title: Discrete entropy: measuring uncertainty in bits
hook: How surprised should you expect to be by the next symbol from a source? Entropy turns a probability distribution into one number: the average information per outcome. It sets the limit on how far a message can be compressed.

symbols.meaning: entropy: average uncertainty of one outcome
contribution of outcome i (0 when p_i = 0)

equation.caption: Shannon writes H = -K \sum p_i \log p_i; choosing K and log base 2 gives bits.

controls.label: Relative weights (normalized to probabilities; only the first n are used)

explorations.title: Certainty carries no information
explorations.predict: If one outcome always happens, how many bits does each observation give?
explorations.observe: H drops to 0; the zero-probability outcomes contribute 0, not NaN.
explorations.why: With p = 1 the term -1·log 1 = 0, and p log p → 0 as p → 0, so nothing is uncertain.

explorations.title: Equal chances maximize uncertainty
explorations.predict: With 4 equally likely outcomes, what is H in bits?
explorations.observe: H = 2 bits, exactly log2 4; make one weight larger and H falls.
explorations.why: Entropy is largest when no outcome is favored; 4 equal outcomes need 2 yes/no questions.

limitation: This page treats independent outcomes from a known distribution; Shannon's full theory also covers sources with memory (Markov processes), not shown here.
misconception: Entropy is not the number of outcomes: adding outcomes with zero probability does not change H.

claims.text: H is zero only when one outcome has probability one.
For n outcomes, H is maximal (log n) when all are equally likely.
The weight sliders and their normalization are a teaching device.
